title: PBOC Pledges Moderately Loose Policy for H2 as De-escalation Signals Sink Oil 5%, Japan Confirms Joint Yen Intervention
subhead: China's central bank committed to timely monetary policy adjustments and panda bond facilitation for the second half, while Trump's call-off of Iran strikes and Monday talks announcement sent Brent below $84. Japan confirmed the first coordinated yen-buying with the US in 15 years.

sections.heading: PBOC Signals Moderately Loose Monetary Policy for H2
sections.body:
China's People's Bank of China pledged at its H2 work conference on August 2 to maintain a moderately loose monetary policy and deploy 'more pragmatic, effective, incremental measures' in the second half of 2026. The central bank said it would adjust policy tools in a timely manner, push down intermediary financing fees, and keep overall social financing costs low, according to the statement posted on its website.

On the structural side, the PBOC said it would facilitate panda bond issuance by foreign entities, deepen local-currency settlement cooperation with overseas central banks, and advance the Cross-border Interbank Payment System. Panda bond issuance topped 160 billion yuan in the first half of 2026. It also pledged to support Shanghai in upgrading cross-border financial services and consolidate Hong Kong as an offshore yuan hub.

Data released at the meeting showed aggregate social financing rose 7.4% year-on-year at end-June, while broad money supply (M2) grew 8%. Lending under the 'five major areas' — technology, green, inclusive, pension, and digital finance — expanded 11% year-on-year, markedly outpacing overall loan growth. The State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) separately pledged to expand forex market access and monitor cross-border capital flows more closely.
sections.whyItMatters: The PBOC is shifting from reactive mode to proactive easing — pledging timely adjustments, lower financing costs, and deeper yuan internationalization. With social financing already growing at 7.4% and targeted lending outpacing total credit, Beijing is trying to offset weak domestic demand while managing capital outflow pressures from the Iran-war-driven commodity shock.

sections.heading: Trump Calls Off Iran Strikes, Announces Monday Talks as Oil Plunges
sections.body:
Oil prices fell sharply on Sunday-Monday after President Donald Trump told US forces to hold off on new strikes against Iran and said negotiations with Tehran would begin on Monday. Brent crude dropped roughly 5% to around $83.70-83.85 per barrel, while WTI fell to about $80.50-80.80, according to AP News and Gulf News. Trump said Middle Eastern countries, including Iran, had asked for additional time to finalize an agreement on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing Iran's nuclear program.

However, Iran rejected Trump's claim that a draft agreement encompassed the full reopening of Hormuz. Iran stated that the waterway could remain shut as long as hostilities continue, according to Business Standard. The gap between Trump's diplomatic optimism and Iran's position underscores how fragile the de-escalation signal remains.

Despite the price drop, three additional maritime incidents have been reported since Saturday, according to Reuters, and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports continues. Gulf News reported that 38 commercial vessels have been redirected under the blockade, which resumed July 14. The blockade targets vessels bound for or departing Iranian ports while keeping Hormuz open to compliant traffic, according to US Central Command.
sections.whyItMatters: The oil selloff reflects markets pricing in de-escalation, but the underlying supply disruption is unchanged: Hormuz transit remains constrained, the US blockade is active, and Iran has not agreed to reopen the waterway. A 5% crude drop on diplomatic hopes can reverse just as quickly if talks falter — as the past five months of conflict have repeatedly demonstrated.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Adds Supply as Saudi Aramco Refinery Hit Complicates Outlook
sections.body:
OPEC+ approved a 188,000 barrels-per-day production increase for September, according to the Financial Express, adding a bearish supply-side factor on top of the de-escalation-driven price drop. The increase is modest relative to the scale of Gulf disruptions but signals the group's willingness to offset some of the lost barrels.

On the demand side, India imported a record 2.8 million barrels per day of Russian crude in July, accounting for 55.3% of total imports, as refiners continued to discount heavily sanctioned-origin barrels. India's crude-buying pattern has effectively become a sanctions-evasion corridor, with Russian crude flowing via ship-to-ship transfers and re-flagged vessels.

Meanwhile, Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery (400,000 bpd capacity) was shut down after a Houthi drone strike, according to regional media. The outage removes a meaningful chunk of Saudi's domestic refining capacity and complicates the kingdom's ability to compensate for Hormuz disruptions with increased product exports.
sections.whyItMatters: The combination of OPEC+ adding supply, Iran talks generating de-escalation hopes, and a 5% price drop might suggest relief — but the Jazan refinery shutdown and continued Hormuz closure mean the physical market remains tight. The 188,000 bpd OPEC+ increase is a fraction of what Hormuz disruption removes from global supply.

sections.heading: Japan Confirms First Joint Yen Intervention With US in 15 Years
sections.body:
Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed on August 3 that the ministry conducted coordinated yen-buying intervention with the US Treasury on Friday — the first such joint action in 15 years, according to CNBC TV18 and the Straits Times. The confirmation came after days of market speculation triggered by a photograph of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's notepad at a Camp David cabinet meeting listing 'Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil' under a 'To Do' heading.

Bloomberg reported that Japan made its largest-ever single-day intervention, spending over $53.7 billion (8.45 trillion yen). The Financial Times reported that the New York Fed sold euros to buy yen on behalf of the Treasury. The yen rebounded from a low of around 164 per dollar to approximately 156-157, a gain of roughly 4% over two days.

Katayama stated the ministry 'will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention.' Bessent described yen movements as 'disorderly' and said the Treasury is ready to keep helping. Trump called the intervention 'a signal of friendship' and said the US would reap 'financial benefit.' Goldman Sachs wrote that further intervention is likely if the yen begins to unwind recent gains. The Bank of Japan held rates at 1% — the highest since 1995 — at its meeting last week.
sections.whyItMatters: The coordinated intervention marks a historic shift in US currency policy — Washington has not bought yen alongside Japan since 2011. The scale ($53.7 billion single-day) and the dual-front approach (Japan buying yen, US selling euros to buy yen) signal that both governments view the yen's weakness as a systemic risk. Whether it holds depends on whether the BOJ tightens further and whether US rates begin to come down — neither of which is imminent.

sections.heading: RBI Set to Hold Rates as Global Risks Cloud India Outlook
sections.body:
The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee begins its August 3-5 meeting with a consensus expectation of a repo rate hold at 5.25% and a 'neutral' policy stance, according to a Mint poll of 10 economists. All 10 respondents expect no rate change, making this meeting about what the RBI says rather than what it does.

Headline inflation accelerated to an 18-month high of 4.4% in June, with food inflation surprising on the upside. The RBI's FY27 inflation forecast stands at 5.1% and GDP growth at 6.6%, with some economists believing Q1 activity has been stronger than anticipated. However, the central bank is expected to adopt a cautious, mildly hawkish tone, with at least four of the 10 economists surveyed expecting a rate hike later in FY27 if crude-driven inflation pressures persist.

On the external front, India's FCNR(B) deposit scheme attracted about $36.73 billion as of August 1, alongside $2.57 billion in overseas foreign currency borrowings and $1.52 billion in external commercial borrowings. The special scheme, open until September 30, is expected to bring in $45-55 billion total, helping support the rupee amid global volatility.
sections.whyItMatters: India is one of the few major economies holding rates steady amid the Iran-war commodity shock, relying instead on foreign-currency inflows to defend the rupee. If oil prices fall sustainably on de-escalation, the RBI gains room to keep rates on hold. If the Hormuz crisis drags on, the 4 of 10 economists forecasting a rate hike later this year could be proven right.

sections.heading: Gold Retreats Toward $4,000 as Safe-Haven Bid Weakens on De-escalation
sections.body:
Spot gold fell to around $3,992-4,061 per ounce on Friday, reversing earlier gains as oil prices retreated, according to BNN Bloomberg. UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo noted that 'lower oil prices' were 'reducing pressure on the Fed to adjust its rates,' which in turn diminished gold's inflation-hedge appeal. Silver traded at $58.43/oz, platinum at $1,602.74, and palladium at $1,256.95.

The gold pullback follows weeks in which the metal hovered near multi-month highs, supported by geopolitical risk and expectations that the Fed would eventually be forced to hike rates to combat war-driven inflation. With Trump calling off Iran strikes and oil dropping 5%, the near-term inflation narrative has softened. Traders are now pricing about an 80% chance of a Fed rate hike in September, according to the CME FedWatch Tool cited by BNN Bloomberg — down from fully priced before the FOMC meeting.

The week ahead brings US nonfarm payrolls on Friday, ISM manufacturing data on Monday, and ISM services on Wednesday — all of which will shape whether the gold retreat continues or reverses. Treasury refunding announcements on Monday and Wednesday will also set tone for yields.
sections.whyItMatters: Gold near $4,000 is still historically elevated, but the shift from inflation-hedge buying to risk-on de-escalation trade shows how quickly the metal can lose support. If oil continues falling and the Fed stays on hold, gold's floor could be tested. If Hormuz talks collapse, the inflation trade re-ignites and gold bounces.

bottomLine: Three things changed this weekend that markets are still processing: Trump called off planned Iran strikes and announced Monday peace talks, sending oil down 5% and Brent below $84; China's PBOC explicitly committed to moderately loose monetary policy with targeted structural tools and panda bond facilitation for H2; and Japan confirmed the first coordinated yen-buying intervention with the US since 2011, with $53.7 billion deployed in a single day. The oil drop is real but fragile — Iran has not agreed to reopen Hormuz, the US blockade continues, and three maritime incidents were reported just since Saturday. The PBOC move is a significant shift in tone from Beijing, signaling that domestic demand weakness now outweighs financial stability concerns. And the yen intervention, while massive, only bought time — the underlying interest-rate gap and energy-cost pressures that drove the yen to 40-year lows remain unchanged. India's RBI will likely hold rates at 5.25% this week, but the de-escalation in oil could give it more room to stay dovish than expected even 48 hours ago.
sources: AP News, Gulf News, Global Times, Straits Times, CNBC TV18, Business Standard, BNN Bloomberg, Seeking Alpha, Morningstar/Dow Jones, Livemint, Financial Express, Bloomberg, Reuters, Nikkei
